messages.content: I want to develop a semantic parser that distinguishes genuine utterance ambiguity from model uncertainty under unseen compositional structures. What is the distinction at the center of that goal?

Genuine utterance ambiguity concerns the utterance itself: more than one interpretation may be valid. Model uncertainty concerns the parser: it may be unsure which interpretation is right, especially when it encounters a compositional structure it has not seen before. The goal is not to treat the parser’s uncertainty as evidence that the utterance has multiple valid interpretations.
So an unfamiliar composition could make the parser hesitate even if the input is unambiguous?

Yes. Unfamiliarity to the parser and ambiguity in the utterance are different things. An input can have a single valid interpretation while the parser is uncertain about it. Conversely, an utterance can genuinely support multiple valid interpretations; that is not merely a description of the parser’s confidence.
How do the independently annotated sets of valid interpretations fit into this?

They provide the reference for evaluating ambiguity detection. The relevant question is what interpretations are valid for the utterance according to those independently annotated sets, not merely how many possibilities the parser considers. The goal specifies their use for evaluating ambiguity-detection F1 on unseen compositions; it does not specify how the annotations are produced.
Is the target simply to perform well at ambiguity detection in general?

The stated target is more specific: achieve ambiguity-detection F1 of at least 0.85 on unseen compositions, using independently annotated sets of valid interpretations. The numerical threshold, the unseen-composition condition, and the annotation basis all matter. This is a goal, not a reported result.
What does F1 tell us in that requirement?

F1 combines precision and recall for the ambiguity-detection task. A target of F1 ≥0.85 therefore concerns the quality of the ambiguity decisions overall, rather than specifying a separate minimum for precision or for recall. The requirement does not give either component its own threshold.
Why emphasize unseen compositional structures rather than just asking whether the parser can recognize ambiguous wording?

That condition makes the distinction especially important. When a composition is unseen, the parser may be uncertain for reasons having to do with its own ability to interpret the input. The intended ambiguity decision still has to reflect whether the utterance genuinely admits multiple valid interpretations, rather than treating compositional novelty itself as ambiguity.
Could a parser meet the detection target yet still mishandle inputs that have only one valid interpretation?

The two requirements address different aspects of performance, so the goal includes a separate safeguard for that case: the parser must match the unambiguous-input execution accuracy of a single-output parser trained on identical data. Ambiguity detection alone would not express that execution-accuracy comparison.
What exactly is the comparison baseline?

It is a single-output parser trained on identical data. The comparison is specifically about execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs. The goal does not give a numerical accuracy target or specify an allowed gap; it says to match that baseline’s unambiguous-input execution accuracy.
Does “identical data” mean the comparison can use whatever training sets are convenient for the two parsers?

No. The wording calls for the single-output parser to be trained on identical data, so the stated comparison holds the training data the same. It does not otherwise prescribe the parsers’ designs or explain how the comparison is to be implemented.
Why specify a single-output parser for that comparison?

It identifies the baseline whose unambiguous-input execution accuracy the semantic parser is expected to match. The requirement does not say that the baseline must detect ambiguity, nor does it specify the form of the new parser’s outputs. Its stated role here is as the execution-accuracy comparator on unambiguous inputs.
Does the goal require the new parser to list every valid interpretation for each utterance?

It does not state that output requirement. It calls for distinguishing genuine ambiguity from model uncertainty and for measuring ambiguity-detection F1 against independently annotated sets of valid interpretations. Those sets are part of the specified evaluation basis, but the goal does not prescribe a particular output format or require an enumeration of every interpretation.
Suppose the parser is unsure about a clear utterance solely because the composition is unfamiliar. Would calling that ambiguous express the intended distinction?

No. That would describe the parser’s uncertainty as though it were genuine utterance ambiguity. The distinction asks whether multiple interpretations are valid for the utterance, not merely whether the parser struggles to choose one under an unseen compositional structure.
And if multiple interpretations really are valid, confidence in just one of them would not make the utterance unambiguous?

Right. The parser’s confidence and the utterance’s valid interpretations are different considerations. Being confident in one reading does not, by itself, establish that no other reading is valid. That is why the independently annotated sets of valid interpretations matter to the ambiguity-detection requirement.
Is the requirement saying the model must never be uncertain on unseen compositions?

No. It asks the parser to distinguish model uncertainty from genuine utterance ambiguity, not to eliminate uncertainty. The measurable ambiguity-detection goal is F1 ≥0.85 on unseen compositions, and the additional requirement concerns execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs relative to the specified single-output baseline.
Should I read the accuracy comparison as another way of measuring ambiguity-detection F1?

No. Ambiguity-detection F1 evaluates the ambiguity distinction against independently annotated sets of valid interpretations on unseen compositions. Unambiguous-input execution accuracy evaluates execution on inputs that are unambiguous and compares it with a single-output parser trained on identical data. The goal requires both, but they are not the same measure.

If I restate the goal, I should keep the ≥0.85 threshold attached to ambiguity detection on unseen compositions, and keep the baseline comparison attached to execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs. Is that precise?

Yes. Keep the independently annotated sets of valid interpretations attached to the ambiguity-detection evaluation as well. The other requirement is to match the unambiguous-input execution accuracy of a single-output parser trained on identical data; no numerical execution-accuracy value is stated.

For the parser proposal, I want to freeze the baseline parser and train an interpretation-set ensemble to flag multiple valid parses supported across independently trained members. How should I understand those two parts together?

The baseline parser would remain fixed while the interpretation-set ensemble is trained. The ensemble’s proposed role is to flag cases with multiple valid parses that have support across independently trained members. Freezing the baseline keeps the comparison parser unchanged; it does not itself determine which utterances are ambiguous.
Does “freeze” mean the ensemble is frozen too?

No. The proposal says to freeze the baseline parser and train the interpretation-set ensemble. It does not say to freeze the ensemble. Nor does it specify the training procedure or any later update schedule.
What is the interpretation set meant to represent here?

It focuses the ensemble on possible parses of an utterance rather than solely on one selected output. The proposed flag concerns multiple valid parses supported across independently trained members. The proposal does not specify a particular representation for those parses or how an interpretation set is assembled.
Is a collection of different guesses from one ensemble member enough to trigger the proposed flag?

That would not capture the stated cross-member condition on its own. The proposal calls for support across independently trained members, not just multiple alternatives from a single member. It does not specify an exact support threshold or a voting rule.
So should every member have to produce the same entire set of parses?

That is not stated. Support across independently trained members is part of the proposal, but it does not define unanimity, identical sets, or a required number of members supporting each parse. Those would be additional design choices.
Why talk about valid parses rather than simply counting every parse the ensemble produces?

Because producing several candidates is not, by itself, the same as identifying genuine utterance ambiguity. The proposal is to flag multiple valid parses with cross-member support. It does not say that every generated candidate is valid, or that disagreement among members alone establishes validity.
Could the members disagree because they are uncertain about an unseen composition, even if only one parse is valid?

Yes, that is a possibility the broader ambiguity-versus-uncertainty distinction makes important. The proposed ensemble should not be described as proving ambiguity merely by displaying disagreement. Its stated flag is for multiple valid parses supported across independently trained members; whether a particular flag is correct would still need to be assessed.
Does independent training guarantee that agreement means the utterance is genuinely ambiguous?

No guarantee is stated. Independent training describes the members whose support the proposal draws on; agreement across them does not logically establish that their parses are valid. The proposal gives a way to seek supporting evidence for multiple parses, not a completed demonstration of ambiguity-detection performance.
What do we know about how the members are trained independently?

Only that they are independently trained members of the interpretation-set ensemble. The proposal does not specify their number, architectures, training data allocation, initialization, or method of combining their outputs.
Would it be accurate to say the fixed baseline is one of those independently trained ensemble members?

The proposal does not say that. It separately names a baseline parser to freeze and an interpretation-set ensemble to train. Treating the baseline as an ensemble member would add a relationship that has not been specified.
Is freezing the baseline a claim that it already has some particular accuracy?
No. Freezing it means keeping that parser fixed in this proposal. It does not report an accuracy value, claim a performance result, or establish that the ensemble matches its execution accuracy.
And has the ensemble already reached the ambiguity-detection goal?

No result is reported here. Training the ensemble and using cross-member support to flag multiple valid parses is a proposal. Whether it achieves the intended ambiguity distinction or any performance target remains an evaluation question.
I want to avoid making the proposal sound as though uncertainty has disappeared. What wording would preserve that distinction?

You could say: “Keep the baseline parser fixed and train an interpretation-set ensemble to flag multiple valid parses supported across independently trained members.” That states the proposed mechanism without saying every disagreement is ambiguity or that uncertainty has been eliminated.
If the ensemble offers several possibilities but support for multiple valid ones is not established across members, is the proposed flag justified?

Not on the condition as stated. Several possibilities alone do not satisfy the proposal’s description of multiple valid parses supported across independently trained members. The proposal does not spell out exactly how that support or validity is determined, so it would be premature to specify a more detailed decision rule.
Then the baseline and ensemble have distinct roles, but neither role settles the empirical outcome?

Exactly. The proposal keeps the baseline parser fixed and trains the interpretation-set ensemble for the cross-member-supported, multiple-valid-parse flag. It specifies those roles, not an observed outcome for ambiguity detection or execution accuracy.
Can cross-member support distinguish genuinely valid alternative parses from disagreement caused by unseen compositional structures?

That is the central question. Support across independently trained members could be informative, but it is not, by itself, proof that the alternatives are valid. Members might support different parses because the utterance genuinely admits them, or because an unseen composition makes the utterance difficult for the models to interpret. The question is whether cross-member support separates those situations reliably.
What would cross-member support actually tell us, then?

It would tell us that support for the candidate parses is not confined to a single trained member. That is different from establishing that the utterance itself has multiple valid interpretations. The evidence comes from the models’ outputs; validity is a property of the interpretations of the utterance.
If independently trained members converge on two parses, doesn’t that make genuine ambiguity likely?

It might make the alternatives worth considering, but convergence does not settle the question. Independent training does not guarantee independent mistakes or guarantee that each supported parse is valid. The distinction matters most when an unseen compositional structure could affect more than one member.
So the word “independently” describes their training, not a guarantee about their judgments?

Exactly. It says something about how the members are trained relative to one another. It does not, on its own, certify their judgments about validity or show that their uncertainty behaves differently on unseen compositions.
Could there also be genuine ambiguity that the members fail to support across the ensemble?

Conceptually, yes. An utterance might admit more than one valid parse even if the members do not provide cross-member support for each one. In that case, the absence of such support would not make the utterance unambiguous. Whether this happens, and how often, is not established by the question.
Then there are two possible mistakes: flagging ambiguity because models struggle, and missing ambiguity because they overlook a valid parse?

Those are the two conceptual risks. Cross-member support could appear for alternatives that are not genuinely valid, while a genuinely valid alternative could lack the required support. Asking whether the signal distinguishes ambiguity from unseen-structure disagreement means asking how well it avoids both kinds of confusion.
Is disagreement among members the same thing as cross-member support for multiple parses?

Not necessarily. Disagreement merely says members differ. Cross-member support for multiple parses says that the alternatives have support extending across independently trained members. Neither description alone establishes that the alternatives are valid; the question is whether the latter provides a useful distinction.
What if all the members are uncertain in a similar way about an unseen composition?

Then their agreement or recurring alternatives could still reflect a shared difficulty rather than ambiguity in the utterance. That is a possibility to keep in view, not a finding about how these members behave. Independent training alone does not rule it out.
Am I asking whether support is evidence, or whether it is a definitive test?

The wording asks whether cross-member support can distinguish the two sources of alternative parses. It can be considered a potential signal, but calling it a definitive test would go beyond what is established. The important unresolved point is whether supported alternatives track genuinely valid parses rather than model responses to unseen compositional structures.
Can you give a general illustration without assuming any particular parser outputs?

Imagine, in the abstract, an utterance for which two interpretations really are valid. Support for both across members would be consistent with genuine ambiguity. Now imagine an utterance with only one valid interpretation whose composition is unfamiliar to the models. If members nevertheless support two candidates, the same observable pattern of support could be misleading. These are illustrations of why the source of the alternatives matters, not claims about observed cases.
So even the same pattern of ensemble support might have different meanings depending on the utterance?

Yes. The pattern concerns what the members support; the ambiguity question concerns what the utterance validly permits. The issue is whether cross-member support aligns closely enough with that latter distinction, particularly when compositional structure is unseen.
Does freezing the baseline parser answer any part of this question?

Freezing the baseline keeps it fixed, but it does not by itself establish that the ensemble’s supported alternatives are valid. The question here is specifically about what can be inferred from support across the independently trained ensemble members when unseen compositions may also produce disagreement.
Should I phrase the concern as ‘agreement might be correlated uncertainty’?

That can convey the concern as a possibility: members trained independently might still show similar uncertainty or mistakes on an unseen structure. It should not be phrased as a demonstrated cause of their behavior. The question remains whether cross-member support identifies genuinely valid alternatives rather than merely recurring model responses.
If one parse has broad support and another has weaker support, does the question tell us which interpretation is valid?

No. It provides no support threshold or rule for deciding validity from relative support. More or less support describes the ensemble’s behavior; it does not automatically settle whether either parse is a valid interpretation of the utterance.
Is it fair to leave the answer open instead of saying the ensemble succeeds or fails?

Yes. The node poses an open question about the proposed signal. The careful formulation is that cross-member support may be relevant evidence, while its ability to separate genuine alternative parses from unseen-composition-driven disagreement has not been established here.

Here is the hypothesis I want to examine: three-of-five support for distinct executable parses achieves ambiguity F1 ≥0.85 against independently annotated interpretation sets on unseen compositions. How should I read that claim?

It is a prediction about an ambiguity-detection signal, not a reported result. The signal is three-of-five support for distinct executable parses. The predicted outcome is ambiguity F1 of at least 0.85, measured against independently annotated interpretation sets on unseen compositions.
What does “three-of-five support” contribute to the hypothesis?

It makes cross-member support concrete: support is sought from three of five members, rather than inferred from a possibility raised by one member alone. The hypothesis does not spell out every detail of how a member’s support is counted, so it is best not to add a more specific voting rule when restating it.
And why say “distinct executable parses” instead of just “different outputs”?

The wording narrows the alternatives under consideration to parses that are distinct and executable. Merely having different outputs would not express either condition. At the same time, executable does not necessarily mean valid as an interpretation of the utterance; that is why comparison with independently annotated interpretation sets remains important.
If a parse is executable, couldn’t I simply count it as a valid interpretation?

Not on the basis of this hypothesis alone. Executability concerns whether the parse can be executed; interpretive validity concerns whether it is a valid reading of the utterance. The hypothesis predicts that support for distinct executable parses will work well as an ambiguity signal when judged against the annotated interpretation sets. It does not equate executability with validity.
Does “distinct” mean that three members must each return a different parse?

That is not specified. “Distinct executable parses” identifies multiple nonidentical parses of interest, while “three-of-five support” specifies a level of member support. The hypothesis does not give a detailed rule for distributing those three supporting members across the parses, so requiring three different outputs from three different members would add an interpretation not stated here.
Is the predicted F1 for finding ambiguity, or for executing parses correctly?

It is specifically ambiguity F1. The hypothesis predicts F1 ≥0.85 for detecting ambiguity against the independently annotated interpretation sets on unseen compositions. It does not state an execution-accuracy result.
What does the annotation comparison keep us from assuming?

It keeps the ensemble’s own outputs from serving as the sole definition of ambiguity. The independently annotated interpretation sets provide the comparison for whether the ambiguity signal corresponds to valid interpretations. Cross-member support and executability are properties of the proposed signal, not substitutes for that reference.
Does the hypothesis say the annotated sets are generated by the five members?
No. It says the interpretation sets are independently annotated. It does not describe an annotation procedure or say that the ensemble members generate those reference sets.
I’m still concerned that an unseen composition could cause several members to support a wrong alternative. Does the three-of-five threshold rule that out?

The hypothesis does not establish that it does. Three-of-five support might be a useful signal, but several members could, in principle, support an alternative that is executable without being a valid interpretation. Whether the resulting ambiguity decisions reach F1 ≥0.85 against the independent annotations on unseen compositions is precisely the predicted outcome, not something the threshold proves by itself.
Could the threshold also fail to flag an utterance that genuinely has multiple valid readings?

Conceptually, yes. If distinct valid readings do not receive the stated support, the signal might not reflect that ambiguity. That possibility is consistent with calling the F1 claim a hypothesis: both unwarranted flags and missed ambiguity could affect ambiguity-detection performance.
Does F1 ≥0.85 mean that at least 85% of ambiguous utterances must be detected?
No. F1 combines precision and recall; the hypothesis gives a threshold for the combined measure, not a separate 85% recall requirement. It also does not separately specify a precision threshold.
Is the ≥ sign important, or can I paraphrase it as ‘around 0.85’?
The ≥ sign is important. The prediction is ambiguity F1 of at least 0.85, not approximately 0.85. A faithful paraphrase should keep the threshold and its direction.
Does the prediction cover familiar structures as well as unseen compositions?

Its stated condition is unseen compositions. It does not make a separate performance claim for familiar structures, and success elsewhere would not by itself establish the predicted F1 under the unseen-composition condition.
If support appears for two executable parses, is the hypothesis saying those two are definitely valid?

No. It proposes that three-of-five support for distinct executable parses will yield the specified ambiguity-detection performance when compared with the independently annotated interpretation sets. The support pattern is a signal to assess, not a guarantee about the validity of every supported parse.
Does this answer the question of whether cross-member support can distinguish genuine alternatives from model disagreement?

It offers a specific, testable answer in the form of a hypothesis: the three-of-five signal for distinct executable parses is predicted to achieve ambiguity F1 ≥0.85 against independently annotated interpretation sets on unseen compositions. It does not yet establish that cross-member support succeeds at making the distinction.
What, then, should remain explicitly uncertain when I discuss it?

Whether the support signal actually tracks genuinely valid alternative interpretations closely enough on unseen compositions to reach the stated F1 threshold. The hypothesis supplies the support level, the distinct-and-executable condition, the annotation-based comparison, and the predicted numerical result; it supplies no observed performance.

Could I state it concisely as: ‘On unseen compositions, distinct executable parses with three-of-five support will achieve ambiguity F1 of at least 0.85 against independently annotated interpretation sets’?

Yes, provided it is clearly presented as a hypothesis rather than a finding. That wording preserves the three-of-five support condition, distinct executable parses, ambiguity F1 ≥0.85, the independently annotated interpretation sets, and the unseen-composition condition.

To examine whether cross-member support distinguishes valid alternatives from disagreement on unseen compositions, I want to independently annotate held-out compositions, train five parsers on baseline data, calibrate three-member support, and compare ambiguity F1 and unambiguous accuracy. What does that plan establish, and what remains to be found out?

It lays out how to examine the question; it does not establish the answer yet. The independent annotations provide a reference for valid interpretations of held-out compositions. The five parsers provide the members whose support can be examined. Calibrating three-member support concerns how that signal is used, and comparing ambiguity F1 and unambiguous accuracy addresses both ambiguity detection and performance on unambiguous inputs. No outcome for either comparison is reported in the plan.
Why annotate the held-out compositions independently?

The ambiguity assessment needs a reference that is not simply the parsers’ own collection of outputs. Independent annotation allows the supported parses to be compared with annotated valid interpretations. Otherwise, agreement among the parsers could be mistaken for evidence of validity without an independent basis for judging it.
Does ‘held-out compositions’ mean we are examining the unfamiliar-composition part of the question?

Yes. The held-out compositions are the part of the plan directed at the concern that unfamiliar compositional structures might produce model disagreement. The plan does not specify which compositions are held out or how the holdout is constructed.
Are the five parsers meant to be trained on different datasets?

That is not stated. The plan says to train five parsers on baseline data. It does not describe different datasets for individual parsers or specify the details of their training. The relevant point here is that there will be five parsers whose support can be examined.
When you say ‘baseline data,’ are you referring to the training data rather than claiming the baseline parser itself is one of the five?

Yes. ‘Train five parsers on baseline data’ identifies the data used for their training. It does not say that the baseline parser is one of the five. The earlier proposal treats the fixed baseline parser and the interpretation-set ensemble as distinct roles.
How should I describe ‘calibrate three-member support’ without inventing a decision rule?

You can say that the plan includes calibrating the use of support from three members among the five parsers. The plan does not specify the calibration procedure, the criterion for counting support, or a rule for how support for distinct parses is combined. Those details should remain open in a description of this plan.
Does calibration itself show that three-member support corresponds to genuine ambiguity?

No. Calibration is a planned step concerning the support signal. Whether that signal corresponds to genuine ambiguity is what the comparison against independent annotations is meant to examine. The word ‘calibrate’ does not imply that the signal has already been validated.
Could I just compare how often the five parsers disagree and call that ambiguity F1?

Not without relating the ambiguity decisions to the independently annotated interpretations. Parser disagreement and genuine utterance ambiguity are the two things the plan is trying to distinguish. Ambiguity F1 concerns the detection decisions judged against the annotation-based reference, rather than a count of disagreement by itself.
What does comparing ambiguity F1 contribute that looking at examples of supported parses would not?

It gives an aggregate measure of ambiguity detection, including the balance between precision and recall. Looking at supported parses can help explain what a signal means in individual cases, but the planned F1 comparison addresses how the ambiguity decisions perform across the evaluation condition. The plan provides no F1 value yet.
Why compare unambiguous accuracy as well?

Because identifying ambiguity should not be considered in isolation from handling inputs with a single valid interpretation. The plan includes unambiguous accuracy alongside ambiguity F1 so both aspects can be compared. In the stated goal, the accuracy comparison is specifically unambiguous-input execution accuracy relative to a single-output parser trained on identical data; this plan does not report that comparison’s result.
If ambiguity F1 looks good, would that automatically tell us unambiguous accuracy is good too?

No. They measure different things. Ambiguity F1 addresses decisions about whether an utterance is ambiguous, while unambiguous accuracy addresses performance on inputs with one valid interpretation. That is why the plan explicitly includes both comparisons rather than treating either as a substitute for the other.
Does the plan say exactly where calibration happens relative to the held-out comparison?

It lists calibration and comparison as planned steps, but it does not specify the data allocation or detailed evaluation protocol for them. It would be adding a procedure to claim that a particular portion of the held-out compositions is used for calibration or that a particular portion is reserved for comparison.
Does independently annotating the held-out compositions mean the five parsers never see any annotation information?

The plan does not state that. Independent annotation describes the reference for the held-out compositions; it does not fully describe what information the parsers use during training or calibration. We can say they are to be trained on baseline data, but not infer a more detailed information-flow rule from this wording alone.
What would the independent annotations help distinguish if several parsers support the same alternative parse?

They would let that alternative be considered against an independently annotated set of valid interpretations. Several parsers supporting it shows cross-member support; the annotations address the separate question of whether it is genuinely a valid interpretation. The plan is designed to compare those two, not to assume they always coincide.
And if the parsers differ on a held-out composition, does the plan assume the disagreement was caused by the structure being unseen?

No. The held-out condition makes that concern relevant, but observing disagreement would not, on its own, establish its cause. The plan asks whether the support signal distinguishes valid alternatives from disagreement associated with unseen compositional structures; it does not assign a cause to any particular disagreement in advance.
Is this a test of the specific three-member-support idea, rather than a general claim that any ensemble will work?

Yes. The plan calls for five parsers and calibration of three-member support, followed by comparisons of ambiguity F1 and unambiguous accuracy. It does not make a claim about every possible ensemble or support rule.
Should I describe the planned comparisons as proving that cross-member support distinguishes ambiguity from uncertainty?

No. Describe them as a way to assess that question. Even before the comparisons are made, the plan distinguishes what will be measured from what is merely hoped for: annotated interpretations supply the reference, and the F1 and accuracy comparisons supply performance measures. Whether the results support the distinction remains unknown.
Can I restate the whole plan without suggesting the experiment has already happened?

Yes: ‘Independently annotate held-out compositions, train five parsers on baseline data, calibrate three-member support, and compare ambiguity F1 and unambiguous accuracy.’ Keeping those as planned actions preserves the open question about whether cross-member support identifies genuinely valid alternative parses rather than disagreement on unseen compositional structures.

For CompSplit-1, I want three annotators to independently label valid executable interpretations for 600 held-out operator-combination utterances, then adjudicate disagreements. Can we unpack exactly what that activity involves without treating it as completed?

Yes. The activity is to build CompSplit-1 from 600 held-out operator-combination utterances. Three annotators independently label which executable interpretations are valid for those utterances, and disagreements are adjudicated. That describes the intended annotation work; it does not report that the labels or adjudications already exist.
Does the number 600 refer to interpretations or utterances?
It refers to utterances: 600 held-out operator-combination utterances. The activity does not specify how many candidate interpretations any particular utterance has.
And does ‘three annotators’ mean three labels total across the collection?
No. It specifies three annotators who independently label valid executable interpretations for the collection. It does not give a total count of interpretations or labels.
What is important about labeling interpretations rather than assigning each utterance a single ambiguity label?

The stated object of annotation is the set of valid executable interpretations. An ambiguity judgment can be informed by whether an utterance has multiple valid interpretations, but simply assigning a yes-or-no ambiguity label would not express the annotation activity as stated.
Is an interpretation included just because it can be executed?

No. The phrase is ‘valid executable interpretations’: executability and validity both matter. An executable interpretation is not automatically a valid reading of the utterance. The activity calls on annotators to label the interpretations that meet the stated description.
Could the annotators label an interpretation they consider valid even if it is not executable?

That would not fit the stated target of valid executable interpretations. The activity does not specify how executability is checked, so we should not invent a checking procedure, but the interpretations being labeled are explicitly described as executable as well as valid.
Why call the 600 utterances ‘held-out’?

That is a stated condition on the utterances in CompSplit-1: they are held-out operator-combination utterances. It identifies the collection being annotated without specifying exactly how it was held out or from which other material.
Does ‘operator-combination’ tell us which operators or combinations are present?
No. It characterizes the utterances as operator-combination utterances, but the activity names no operators, combinations, or example utterances. Those details should not be inferred from the label.
What does independent annotation mean at this stage?

It means the three annotators label the valid executable interpretations independently before their disagreements are adjudicated. Their initial labels are not simply one shared judgment. The activity does not prescribe a more detailed annotation workflow.
If all three annotators make the same judgment, is adjudication still the point of that case?

The stated adjudication step concerns disagreements. Where there is no disagreement, there is no conflicting judgment to reconcile on that basis. The activity does not spell out any additional review rule for cases of agreement.
If their judgments differ, should I assume majority vote settles it?

No. ‘Adjudicate disagreements’ does not specify majority vote. It says that disagreements are to be resolved through adjudication, but it does not identify who adjudicates, what rule they use, or how a final interpretation set is recorded.
Could disagreement concern which interpretations are valid, rather than merely whether an utterance is ambiguous?

Yes. Because the annotators label valid executable interpretations, they could disagree over whether a particular interpretation belongs among those labeled valid. The activity does not restrict disagreement to a single utterance-level ambiguity decision.
Does adjudication mean one annotator’s initial label was necessarily careless?

No. A disagreement is a difference in judgments that needs adjudication; its existence does not establish why it arose or characterize any annotator’s work. The activity does not state causes of disagreement.
Could I say CompSplit-1 already contains adjudicated sets of interpretations?

Not from this activity statement. It says to build CompSplit-1 by having three annotators independently label valid executable interpretations for the 600 utterances and adjudicating disagreements. It does not report completion or provide the resulting sets.
Are we claiming every one of the 600 utterances has more than one valid executable interpretation?

No. The activity specifies what the annotators will label, not that every utterance is ambiguous. It gives neither the number of valid interpretations per utterance nor the proportion of utterances with multiple valid interpretations.
What if an utterance has only one valid executable interpretation? Does it still belong in the stated annotation activity?

The activity does not require multiple valid interpretations for inclusion. Its scope is 600 held-out operator-combination utterances, for which the annotators label valid executable interpretations. It does not predetermine the annotation outcome for any utterance.
Does the activity specify how candidate interpretations reach the annotators?

No. It does not say whether candidates are supplied, generated, or elicited in some other way. The specified work is independent labeling of valid executable interpretations and adjudication of disagreements; a candidate-presentation method would be an additional detail.
Is there a performance result or agreement score attached to CompSplit-1 here?

No. There is no reported annotator agreement score, adjudication outcome, ambiguity F1, or parser accuracy in this activity. It specifies the construction of CompSplit-1, including its size, utterance type, independent labeling by three annotators, and disagreement adjudication.

Let me restate it: build CompSplit-1 using 600 held-out operator-combination utterances; have three annotators independently identify the valid executable interpretations; adjudicate where their labels disagree. Is that faithful?

Yes. That preserves the name CompSplit-1, the 600 held-out operator-combination utterances, three independent annotators, the focus on valid executable interpretations, and the adjudication of disagreements, without implying that the activity has already been completed.
What exactly does CompSplit-1 contain?

CompSplit-1 contains 600 held-out operator-combination utterances. For each utterance, it contains three independent interpretation-set annotations and adjudicated executable gold sets. Those are the contents specified for the artifact; no parser performance results are included in that description.
When you say three annotations each, is that three for the whole collection or three for every utterance?
Three for every utterance. The word “each” attaches to the 600 utterances, so each one has three independent interpretation-set annotations.
Are those annotations just three yes-or-no judgments about ambiguity?

No. They are described as interpretation-set annotations. That is more specific than a single yes-or-no ambiguity judgment: the annotations concern interpretations associated with an utterance. The artifact description does not prescribe the annotations’ storage format.
Does independent mean the three annotations must agree?

No. Independence describes the annotations, not their agreement. CompSplit-1 contains the three annotations as well as adjudicated executable gold sets; its description does not say how often the independent annotations agree or disagree.
How should I distinguish an annotation from an adjudicated gold set?

The three independent annotations preserve separate interpretation-set judgments for an utterance. The adjudicated executable gold set is the adjudicated reference associated with it. They should not be described as three identical copies of the gold set, and the artifact description does not specify the rule used to adjudicate differences.
Does ‘adjudicated’ let us infer that a majority vote determined the gold sets?
No. It tells us the executable gold sets were adjudicated, but it does not identify a voting rule, an adjudicator, or a detailed reconciliation procedure.

I want to audit Anchored SingleSet v2’s CompSplit-2 ambiguity F1, unambiguous execution, and baseline-output disagreement against the gold sets and the cascade’s 0.85/91%. How should I separate those checks?

The audit has three distinct measures. Assess v2’s ambiguity decisions against the CompSplit-2 gold interpretation sets to determine ambiguity F1. Assess its execution on unambiguous inputs and compare that result with the cascade’s 91% unambiguous execution. Separately, measure how often v2’s outputs disagree with baseline outputs on unambiguous inputs. The cascade’s ambiguity-F1 comparator is 0.85. This activity does not report any of v2’s results.
Does the cascade’s 0.85 refer to execution?
No. The cascade’s 0.85 is ambiguity F1; its 91% is unambiguous execution. Those are the two cascade figures named for comparison, and they should stay attached to their respective measures.
Are the CompSplit-2 gold sets the same thing as the cascade’s predictions?

No. The gold sets are the adjudicated interpretation reference. The cascade’s outputs are predictions from a system whose reported ambiguity F1 and unambiguous execution provide comparators. Treating its predictions as gold would confuse the reference with an approach being evaluated.
How do the gold sets help with the ambiguity-F1 audit?

They provide a reference for which interpretations are valid for CompSplit-2 utterances. V2’s ambiguity decisions can be assessed against that reference to calculate ambiguity F1. The fact that v2 has prediction logs does not itself tell us what its F1 is.
Do the gold sets also establish which inputs count as unambiguous?

They provide the interpretation reference for that distinction: an unambiguous input has a single valid interpretation in the relevant gold set. The activity does not specify a more detailed scoring protocol, but the input condition should not be defined solely by what v2 predicts.
Could I calculate unambiguous execution only on inputs v2 declines to flag as ambiguous?
That could omit genuinely unambiguous inputs on which v2 issues a false ambiguity alert. The stated measure concerns execution on unambiguous inputs, not just inputs v2 classifies as unambiguous.
What does comparing v2’s execution with 91% establish if they happen to match?

Conditionally, equal reported execution results would show that v2 matches the cascade’s 91% aggregate unambiguous-execution figure. It would not show that v2 and the cascade executed exactly the same individual inputs correctly. No v2 execution result is reported in this activity.
Would matching the 91% figure also prove v2 preserves every baseline output?

No. Execution accuracy and exact output agreement are different properties. That is why baseline-output disagreement is a separate audit measure: equal aggregate execution accuracy cannot establish that v2 retains each baseline output on unambiguous inputs.
What exactly is being counted as baseline-output disagreement?

It concerns unambiguous inputs for which v2’s output differs from the baseline’s output. The activity does not supply a disagreement rate or specify a finer-grained output-comparison convention. It should not be relabeled as an execution-error rate.
If v2 differs from the baseline on an unambiguous input, must v2 be wrong?

Not necessarily. A difference in outputs does not by itself tell us which output, if either, executes correctly. The audit measures disagreement separately from execution so that one is not assumed to determine the other.
Could baseline-output disagreement be measured by checking whether v2 agrees with the cascade instead?

No. The specified disagreement is with the baseline’s output. Cascade predictions can provide a system comparison, but agreement or disagreement with the cascade is not a substitute for comparing v2 directly with the baseline on unambiguous inputs.
Does the cascade’s 0.85 ambiguity F1 tell us v2’s ambiguity F1 in advance?

What if v2 has the same F1 as the cascade but a different baseline-output disagreement rate?

That is conceptually possible. Ambiguity F1 and baseline-output disagreement assess different behavior. Matching 0.85 F1 would not establish how frequently v2 changes baseline outputs on unambiguous inputs. This activity does not say that such a match occurs.
Could I use the cascade’s 91% as the denominator when calculating output disagreement?

No. The 91% is an unambiguous-execution result, not a count of inputs or a denominator for output disagreement. The activity does not specify the disagreement calculation beyond its scope: baseline outputs on unambiguous inputs.

How do the ambiguity F1 scores compare?
The cascade’s ambiguity F1 is 0.85, which is 0.01 F1 points higher than anchored SingleSet v2’s 0.84 on CompSplit-2. That comparison is about ambiguity detection, not execution or output agreement.
Does the cascade also have higher unambiguous execution?
No. Both are reported at 91% unambiguous execution. The difference between their reported results is in ambiguity F1, not in the aggregate execution percentage.
Does equal execution at 91% mean they handled precisely the same unambiguous utterances correctly?
Not necessarily. Equal aggregate percentages do not establish that the two approaches succeeded and failed on the same individual utterances. This finding gives no case-by-case execution comparison.
What exactly does the 2% baseline-output disagreement tell us?

On 2% of unambiguous inputs, anchored SingleSet v2 produced an output different from the baseline’s. That is an exact-output comparison with the baseline, not a measure of how often v2 executed an input incorrectly.
Can I say the remaining 98% of unambiguous outputs matched the baseline?

For the reported binary agreement-versus-disagreement comparison, yes: a 2% disagreement rate corresponds to 98% agreement on the unambiguous inputs assessed. It does not mean 98% execution accuracy; v2’s reported unambiguous-execution result is 91%.
Is every output in that 2% necessarily an error by v2?
No. Disagreement shows that the outputs differ. It does not say which output, if either, is correct in each case. The 2% should not be relabeled as an execution-error rate.
Could the baseline be wrong in a disagreement case?

That is possible in principle. The finding reports disagreement with baseline outputs, not a correctness judgment for those particular cases. It gives no breakdown of which system is correct when their outputs differ.
Then why keep the 2% separate from the 91%?

They answer different questions. The 2% asks how often v2’s output differs from the baseline’s on unambiguous inputs. The 91% asks how often v2 executes unambiguous inputs correctly. Two systems can match in aggregate execution accuracy without producing the same output on every input.
Could I subtract the 2% disagreement from the 91% execution figure?
No. They are percentages for different outcomes, not parts of one error total. Subtracting them would not produce a meaningful additional execution or agreement score.
Does this finding give an ambiguity false-alert rate for v2?
No. Its reported ambiguity-detection measure is F1 of 0.84. Baseline-output disagreement of 2% is not a false-ambiguity-alert rate, and F1 alone does not supply one.
Does the lower F1 tell us whether v2 made more false alerts than the cascade?

Not necessarily. That would interpret the value as recall. The reported 0.84 is F1, which combines precision and recall; neither component is given separately.
Is the 2% disagreement an F1 score expressed as a percentage?
No. It is a rate of disagreement between anchored SingleSet v2 and baseline outputs on unambiguous inputs. It measures neither ambiguity F1 nor ambiguity-detection accuracy.
Does the finding tell us how many individual outputs differed from the baseline?
It reports a rate of 2% but no count of unambiguous inputs used for that comparison. Without the relevant count, it should not be converted into an exact number of differing outputs.

No. The decision says v2 reduces disagreement. “Reduces” should not be strengthened to “eliminates,” and the decision does not claim exact agreement with the baseline on every unambiguous input.

Its ambiguity F1 is below the 0.85 threshold. That is the stated shortfall for anchored v2. It does not, by itself, identify whether false ambiguity alerts, missed genuine ambiguity, or both account for the score.

Would ‘v2 is worse than v1 in every respect’ be a fair summary?
No. V2 is explicitly described as reducing baseline-output disagreement. The decision identifies a trade-off relevant to the choice, not an across-the-board ranking of the two SingleSet versions.
